meta.title: Who really said "The Main Thing Is Honesty. If You Can Fake That, You've Got It Made"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Celeste Holm didn't coin it — in April 1962 she quoted an unnamed actor. Quote Investigator finds no evidence for Groucho Marx or Samuel Goldwyn either.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The Main Thing Is Honesty. If You Can Fake That, You've Got It Made'?
meta.ogDescription: She got it into print first — but she was quoting an actor she wouldn't name. The 1962 trail behind a joke nobody has ever owned.

answer.label: Not Celeste Holm — a line she quoted from an unnamed actor
answer.authorDates: Quoted by Celeste Holm, April 1962 · never identified
answer.sourceLine: The joke first reaches print in Leonard Lyons’s syndicated column The Lyons Den on 6 April 1962, where Celeste Holm repeats it as something she had heard another actor say during a panel on where acting was heading. She named no one, and never claimed the line as her own. Quote Investigator ↗ finds no earlier appearance, traces many of the later versions to a 1969 retelling in Life, and concludes the coiner remains unknown — and the familiar wording, “The main thing is honesty. If you can fake that, you’ve got it made,” is a later polish of it, not anything Holm is recorded as saying.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — Holm is the first person on record repeating it, but she was quoting someone else, and no one has ever identified him.

source.excerpt: Honesty. That’s the thing in the theater today. Honesty … and just as soon as I can learn to fake that, I’ll have it made.
trail: 6 April 1962 — the earliest appearance located by Quote Investigator ↗: Leonard Lyons’s syndicated column The Lyons Den quotes Celeste Holm quoting an unnamed actor. Lyons wrote the column six days a week from 1934 to 1974, first for the New York Post ↗.

25 April 1969 — an actor’s version appears in Life magazine: “the most important thing for an actor is honesty … And when you learn how to fake that, you’re in.” The issue is on Google Books ↗; the citation is QI’s ↗.

1980 — two different credits land in the same year. George Burns prints a version in The Third Time Around (Putnam), catalogued at the Internet Archive ↗, and Murphy’s Law Book Two hands a ‘sincerity’ variant to Jean Giraudoux without a source — the sole reference Wikiquote can offer for it ↗.

1982 onward — the line is printed as Samuel Goldwyn’s, then as Groucho Marx’s, then simply as an old showbiz proverb. QI ↗ finds no substantive evidence for either man and leaves the coiner anonymous.
source.excerptNote: This is the sentence as Quote Investigator ↗ transcribes it from the 1962 column. Holm was speaking on a panel about trends in show business and offered it as something she had heard an actor say — note that it is not the modern wording, and that the “I” in it is not her.

source.rightsNote: The famous wording — “The main thing is honesty. If you can fake that, you’ve got it made” — has no identified author and no identified first publication, so no copyright status can honestly be asserted for it. The oldest documented text is a different sentence: an unnamed actor’s remark as printed in a 1962 newspaper column, an item whose own rights would sit with the column and its syndicate rather than with any speaker.

author.name: Celeste Holm
author.heading: About Celeste Holm
author.metaLine: 1917–2012 · American stage, film and television actress
author.bio: Celeste Holm won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for Gentleman’s Agreement (1947) and was nominated twice more, for Come to the Stable and All About Eve; on Broadway she originated Ado Annie in Oklahoma! in 1943, and she later carried her own television series. Her connection to this quotation is real but indirect: in April 1962 she was the first person on record to repeat it in public, talking about the vogues in acting. She credited it to another actor and did not name him — which is exactly why the line has floated free of an author ever since, collecting famous names as it went.

misattribution.heading: Five names, none of them the author
misattribution.intro: This line has been handed round for sixty years, and almost every famous name attached to it was attached after the fact. Quote Investigator ↗ dates each hop.

items.why: She is the reason the line survives — but the 1962 column has her quoting another actor, unnamed, while discussing trends in acting. QI ↗ presents her as the earliest known relayer and explicitly does not credit her with coining it.

Burns put a version in his third memoir, The Third Time Around (Putnam, 1980) — “you’ve got to be honest. And if you can fake that, you’ve got it made.” QI ↗ calls that a late date and credits the book with popularising the saying rather than originating it; the memoir is catalogued at the Internet Archive ↗.

The “secret of life is honesty and fair dealing” form turns up credited to Groucho in a 1989 business-ethics column. QI ↗ states that attributions to Marx are not supported by evidence, noting only that he was alive while the expression was circulating.
Printed as a Goldwyn line in a 1982 journal epigraph. Goldwyn is a magnet for invented one-liners, and QI ↗ finds no substantive support for ascribing it to him.
A ‘sincerity’ variant was attached to the French playwright in Arthur Bloch’s Murphy’s Law Book Two (1980) with no citation, and Wikiquote still files it under Attributed ↗ on that single reference.

misattribution.truthLine: The oldest documented owner of this joke is an actor nobody has ever named. Quote Investigator ↗ found it in print on 6 April 1962 already being quoted second-hand, and concludes the coiner remains anonymous.

context.heading: Why nobody owns this joke
lead: It is a very hard line to attribute, because it is a very easy line to have overheard. The 1962 column does not present it as a bon mot from a famous actress; it presents Celeste Holm relaying something going around the profession — a working actor’s crack about a fashion in acting that had already curdled into a mannerism. Backstage jokes have no bylines. This one entered print already second-hand, and it never acquired an owner.

What it acquired instead was a series of plausible hosts. Quote Investigator ↗ tracks the drift across two decades: an actor says it about acting in 1969, George Burns puts a version in a memoir in 1980, a paperback of aphorisms hands it to a French playwright the same year, and by the late 1980s it is being printed as Groucho. Each hop swapped ‘honesty’ for ‘sincerity’ or the reverse, and each hop made the wording a little crisper and the source a little vaguer.
context.detailsSummary: How the wording changed on its way to the meme
detailsBody: The 1962 text is loose and conversational — “Honesty. That’s the thing in the theater today. Honesty … and just as soon as I can learn to fake that, I’ll have it made.” It is a complaint about a trend, not an epigram.

By 1980 George Burns’s memoir has it tightened to “To be a fine actor, when you’re playing a role you’ve got to be honest. And if you can fake that, you’ve got it made” — still tied to acting. The meme version drops the theatre entirely and turns it into a general rule about life, which is what lets it be pinned on comedians, movie moguls and playwrights alike.
context.pull: Holm was not confessing. She was reporting a joke that was already going around.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's earliest located evidence is a 6 April 1962 Leonard Lyons column ('The Lyons Den', Morning Advocate, Baton Rouge, p. 2-A col. 2) in which Celeste Holm quotes an unnamed actor: 'Honesty. That's the thing in the theater today. Honesty … and just as soon as I can learn to fake that, I'll have it made.' QI concludes the coiner remains anonymous, that George Burns's 1980 memoir The Third Time Around (p. 189) popularised it, and that attributions to Groucho Marx and Samuel Goldwyn are not supported by evidence. It also documents the 1969 Life version, the 1980 Murphy's Law Book Two credit to Jean Giraudoux, the 1982 Goldwyn epigraph in Critical Inquiry, the 1989 Management Today Groucho credit and Daniel Schorr's 2003 recollection.

Celeste Holm lived 29 April 1917 – 15 July 2012, was American, won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for Gentleman's Agreement (1947) with further nominations for Come to the Stable and All About Eve, and originated Ado Annie in Oklahoma! (1943). The article contains no quotations attributed to her.
Leonard Lyons (1906–1976) wrote the syndicated column 'The Lyons Den' for the New York Post six days a week from 1934 until his retirement in 1974.

Wikiquote's Jean Giraudoux page lists 'The secret of success is sincerity. Once you can fake that you've got it made' under its Attributed section, sourced only to Arthur Bloch's Murphy's Law Book Two (1980), p. 47, with a note that comparable phrases became part of George Burns's routine.
The Internet Archive holds a catalogue record for George Burns's memoir The Third Time Around, published by Putnam, New York, in 1980 (219 pages), matching the edition Quote Investigator cites.

This Google Books record is the 25 April 1969 issue of Life magazine — the issue Quote Investigator cites for the 1969 actor's version of the remark. (The 'fake that' snippet itself was not reproducible through this record; the quoted wording is taken from QI's transcription.)
Wikiquote has no article for Celeste Holm (HTTP 404), so no Wikiquote sourced/misattributed section exists for this line under her name.

Wikiquote's Groucho Marx page does not contain 'The secret of life is honesty and fair dealing. If you can fake that, you've got it made' in any section — checked so as not to assert a Wikiquote misattribution label that does not exist.
Wikiquote's George Burns page does not contain the 'if you can fake that' line — checked so the Burns credit rests only on QI's citation of his 1980 memoir, not on Wikiquote.
